## Abstract

This report presents global projections of materials use and their environmental consequences, providing a quantitative outlook to 2060 at the global, sectoral and regional levels for 61 different materials (biomass resources, fossil fuels, metals and non-metallic minerals). It explains the economic drivers determining the decoupling of economic growth and materials use, and assesses how the projected shifts in sectoral and regional economic activity influence the use of different materials. The projections include both primary and secondary materials, which provides a deeper understanding of what drives the synergies and trade-offs between extraction and recycling.

The report projects a doubling of global primary materials use between today and 2060. Population and converging per capita income growth drive the growth in materials use. However, structural change, especially in non-OECD countries, and technology improvements partially dampen that growth. Metals and non-metallic minerals are projected to grow more rapidly than other types of materials.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The OECD is a unique forum where governments work together to address the economic, social and environmental challenges of globalisation. The OECD is also at the forefront of efforts to understand and to help governments respond to new developments and concerns, such as corporate governance, the information economy and the challenges of an ageing population. The Organisation provides a setting where governments can compare policy experiences, seek answers to common problems, identify good practice and work to co-ordinate domestic and international policies.

The OECD member countries are: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Chile, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States. The European Union takes part in the work of the OECD.

OECD Publishing disseminates widely the results of the Organisation’s statistics gathering and research on economic, social and environmental issues, as well as the conventions, guidelines and standards agreed by its members.

Photo: Ben Gonzales

Laurence Gonzales is the son of a Mexican biophysicist and an Irish-German woman with a flair for poetry. His first poem was published in Poetry Magazine in 1970, followed by short stories and other poems published in the literary magazines of the time. His career took off when he switched from poetry and fiction to nonfiction.

As early as 1973, he had decided to bring together the worlds of science and poetry to create a new kind of nonfiction. In it, the reader would be transported as in poetry to a world of the author's impressionistic perceptions and imagination. The reader would say, "I felt like I was there."

But at the same time, an experience of real life and true scientific revelation would overlay the essay. The reader would also say, "I never realized that." And would be enlightened.

After thirty years of research and experimentation, he brought those elements together in Deep Survival: Who Lives, Who Dies, and Why. That book created a genre, much imitated, and has remained a consistent best seller since its publication in 2003.

Along the way, his unique style of journalism won him many awards, including two National Magazine Awards and the Montaigne Medal.

Another achievement in his pursuit of this new approach to factual writing was Flight 232: A Story of Disaster and Survival. The first complete reconstruction of the fatal crash of a modern airliner, it was called "A kind of miracle" by Michael Korda and "a new masterpiece" by Richard Rhodes. It represented a landmark in journalism, penetrating an unseen and deadly realm of our daily lives, never before revealed, to demonstrate the beating heart of human compassion within.

His most recent novel is Lucy. His most recent nonfiction book is Isolato: An Intimate Portrait of Cormac McCarthy--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Books Written by Richard Feynman

Richard Feynman won a Nobel Prize, cracked safes at Los Alamos, played drums in a samba band and worked out on live television why the Challenger came apart. What he almost never did was sit down and write a book. Around twenty titles carry his name, and nearly every one of them was assembled by somebody else out of a taped lecture course, a week of conversation, or a box of letters. This page has all of them, what each one actually is, who put it together, and which to read first.

Quick answer

Around twenty books carry Richard Feynman’s name, published between 1961 and 2005, and he wrote almost none of them as books. He lectured, he talked, he answered letters, and other people — two colleagues, a drumming partner, his daughter — turned that into print, most of it after he died. Which is why the number you get depends on what you are willing to call a book by him. What each one is, and who assembled it → If you have never read him, start with Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985).

## Where to Start with Richard Feynman

If you have never read him
→ Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985). The anecdotes, in his talking voice, no physics required.

If you want the mind rather than the man
→ The Character of Physical Law (1965). Seven short lectures on what a law of nature is. The BBC recordings are online, so you can watch him give them.

If you want to understand what he actually won the Nobel for
→ QED (1985). His own work, explained without mathematics, by him.

If you are studying physics
→ The Feynman Lectures on Physics (1964–1966), free in full from Caltech. Buy the paper copies if you are going to live in them.

If physics is not the point for you
→ The Meaning of It All (1999) on doubt and society, or Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track (2005), his letters. My best essays to read list goes further in the same direction.

If you only have an hour
→ The Pleasure of Finding Things Out (1999) and read one piece. It is built for that.

## Summary and Study Guide

### Overview

Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman!: Adventures of a Curious Character is the first memoir of Nobel Prize-winning nuclear physicist Richard Feynman, published in 1985. The book is directed primarily at non-scientists, and the anecdotes Feynman recalls concentrate on explaining how he came to have a reputation as an eccentric who craved adventure and mischief. The conversational tone of the autobiography derives in part from the way it was produced; most of the text is transcribed from tape-recorded conversations with his friend Ralph Leighton, who shared Feynman’s hobby as a musician and was the son of one of Feynman’s colleagues at the California Institute of Technology.
